short: A secretive mystery cult centred on the god Mithras spread through army camps and ports.
full:
Worship of Mithras as a distinct Roman mystery cult emerged around the later first century AD, likely in Rome itself, drawing on the name and some imagery of an older Persian deity without being a direct continuation of Zoroastrian practice. Its underground temples, mithraea, cluster in frontier garrisons and trading ports such as Ostia, spread along the Rhine and Danube by soldiers and merchants who carried initiation from posting to posting. Members progressed through seven ranks in secret rites centred on a bull-slaying image, open only to men.

The cult never had public temples or a unified priesthood, but by the third century it counted senators among its initiates and had become one of paganism's most vigorous competitors with Christianity. It declined sharply after Theodosius's edicts against sacrifice closed temples in the 390s; mithraea were abandoned or deliberately desecrated, and the cult had effectively vanished within a generation.
